title: Measuring change

draft.title: Measuring change
card: Historians judge a movement by asking how far it reached its goals. To do this they compare what it wanted with what actually happened.
the changes seen soon after a movement, such as a new law or a leader stepping down.
the effects seen years or decades later, such as changed attitudes or lasting inequality.

A movement can win some goals and not others. Some things change, such as laws, while others stay the same, such as everyday attitudes. So historians rarely judge a movement a complete success or failure.
draft.remember: Judge a movement by its goals, and look at what changed and what stayed the same, soon and later.

a.q: A movement won a new law in 1965, but unfair treatment in daily life continued for decades. How would a historian judge this?
opts: As a partial success, with change and continuity
As a complete success, because a law was passed
As a complete failure, because unfairness continued
As having no effect, because attitudes stayed the same
a.why: The law is a short-term change, while unfair treatment shows continuity in the long term. Together they point to partial success. Calling it complete success ignores the unfairness that remained.
a.clue: Look at both what changed and what did not.

b.q: A student says a 1970s workers' movement failed because it did not win every demand it made. Which response is the strongest historical judgement?
opts: Compare its demands with the outcomes, short and long term
Accept the claim, since unmet demands mean failure
Count only the laws passed in the first year
Judge it by how many people joined the marches
b.why: Historians weigh goals against outcomes, in both the short and long term. Failing to win every demand does not make a movement a failure. Counting first-year laws or marchers covers only part of the evidence.
b.clue: A fair judgement looks at goals and results over time.

a.best: As a partial success, with change and continuity

b.best: Compare its demands with the outcomes, short and long term

problems.detail: The question asks for the 'strongest historical judgement', but the intended option is a method (compare demands with outcomes), not a judgement. It is also the only option that echoes the card's phrase 'short and long term', and it is slightly the longest, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card, remember line and question a are accurate and fit the point. Question b's intended answer is a method rather than the 'judgement' the question asks for, and it stands out by repeating the card's 'short and long term' wording.

opts: As a partial success, with change and continuity

b.q: In the 1970s, miners in a country town demanded safer mines and higher pay. Safety rules came in within a year, but pay stayed low for ten years. Which judgement fits best?
opts: It partly succeeded: safety improved but pay stayed low
It failed, because it did not win every demand it made
It fully succeeded, because safety rules came in quickly
It had no effect, because pay stayed low for ten years
b.why: The safety rules are a change, while low pay shows continuity, so the movement reached some of its goals but not all. Calling it a failure because one demand was not met ignores the change it did win, and historians rarely judge a movement a complete failure.
b.clue: Check each demand on its own: was it met or not?

a.best: As a partial success, with change and continuity

b.best: It partly succeeded: safety improved but pay stayed low
